ford-pinto-1970.summary: In September 1970 Ford launched the Pinto with a fuel tank that burst in rear crashes; a Ford memo later read as pricing deaths against repairs was a 1973 submission to NHTSA on a proposed rollover rule, and Pinto fire rates ran near its class. Beginning in 1973, Ford’s recall office received field reports of Pintos consumed by fire after low-speed rear-end collisions, and its internal reviews twice found no actionable issue; in 1974 the Center for Auto Safety petitioned NHTSA for a recall without success. Mark Dowie’s August 1977 Mother Jones article “Pinto Madness” drew wide attention, accusing Ford of trading lives for profit.

future-shock-1970.summary: In 1970 the Tofflers' Future Shock argued change had grown too swift for people to absorb; it sold millions of copies. It defines future shock as a psychological state of individuals and whole societies, “too much change in too short a period of time,” arguing that accelerating change from industrial to “super-industrial” society leaves people disconnected and suffering “shattering stress and disorientation.” It popularized the term “information overload” and was widely translated.

grontvedt-salmon-farming-hitra-1970.summary: On 28 May 1970 brothers Ove and Sivert Grontvedt place salmon smolt in a floating open net pen at Hitra island off Trondelag, and in 1971 harvest the first successful generation of farmed Atlantic salmon, after sea-cage trials in Norway through the 1960s. Fish survive winter and reach market size in two years, proving open-sea cages cheaper than shore tanks. Norway's government limits licenses to small coastal owners in 1973, then liberalizes in 1991, and Norway becomes the largest producer; FAO records farmed Atlantic salmon above one million tonnes a year worldwide, over 90 percent of the farmed salmon market, with the industry spreading to Scotland, Faroe Islands, Canada, Chile and Tasmania.

A breeding program begun by Harald Skjervold in 1971 at Sunndalsora raised growth rate within generations, and oil-adjuvant vaccines in the 1990s cut antibiotic use sharply. hybrid-4-cotton-surat-1970.summary: At Main Cotton Research Station, Surat, plant breeder C. T. Patel of Gujarat Agricultural University releases Hybrid-4 in 1970, a cross of two upland cotton lines whose seed is produced by hand emasculation and pollination of every flower. No cotton hybrid had been grown commercially anywhere before. Hybrids yield about half again as much lint as open-pollinated varieties, and cheap skilled labour in Gujarat and Maharashtra makes hand pollination affordable: one worker handles 250 to 400 flowers a day. Hybrid seed companies grow from this base, and when Bt cotton arrives in 2002 it is sold as hybrids, so Indian farmers must buy seed every season. By 2020 hybrids cover over half of India's cotton area.

indian-patents-act-1970.summary: Parliament passed Patents Act 1970, in force from 1972, replacing colonial 1911 law. For food, medicine and chemicals it granted patents only on manufacturing processes, not products, with terms cut to seven years and compulsory licences available. Following Ayyangar committee report of 1959, it reasoned that product monopolies kept drug prices among highest in world while serving foreign firms. Indian companies such as Cipla, Ranbaxy and Dr Reddy's reverse engineered new molecules by alternative routes and built a chemistry-based industry that made India leading exporter of low cost generics. TRIPS obligations forced return to product patents in 2005, with Section 3(d) limits on evergreening.

leloir-sugar-nucleotides-nobel-1970.summary: In 1970 Luis Federico Leloir received his Nobel Prize in Chemistry for identifying sugar nucleotides and their role in building carbohydrates. Working from 1947 at Instituto de Investigaciones Bioquímicas Fundación Campomar, housed in a converted house in Buenos Aires with second-hand equipment, Leloir, Ranwel Caputto, Carlos Cardini, Raúl Trucco and Alejandro Paladini isolated glucose 1,6-bisphosphate and uridine diphosphate glucose (UDPG) in 1949 and 1950, showing how cells transfer activated sugars to make glycogen, starch and other polysaccharides. Enrico Cabib's Science report in 1970 described this award; Leloir's own 1983 memoir with Paladini recounts his discovery. His laboratory trained Argentine biochemists for decades, with Houssay's institute as its model.

By 1974, after James Lighthill’s critique and congressional pressure, US and British governments had stopped funding undirected AI research.

operation-flood-amul-1970.summary: In 1970 India launched Operation Flood, linking village dairy cooperatives to cities (sources date its NDDB implementation from 1972 to 1996); in 1998 India passed America as the world's largest milk producer. It created a national milk grid linking farmers to consumers in over 700 towns and cities, cutting out middlemen; its first phase was financed by selling skimmed milk powder and butter oil donated by the European Economic Community. Verghese Kurien, NDDB chairman, was later recognized as its architect, and within 30 years it doubled milk per person.

China financed and supported it as a turnkey undertaking costing US$406 million, its largest single foreign-aid project at that time, and on completion it was sub-Saharan Africa’s longest railway.

uncanny-valley-1970.summary: In 1970 roboticist Masahiro Mori proposed that near-human robots repel us until they look fully human. Affinity drops into revulsion when an object approaches but does not reach human likeness, and recovers once it becomes indistinguishable from a person. He called this dip bukimi no tani; Jasia Reichardt translated it literally as “uncanny valley” in her 1978 book Robots: Fact, Fiction, and Prediction. It now frames debate over animatronics, lifelike dolls, 3D animation and AI-generated faces.

victoria-compulsory-seat-belt-law-1970.summary: Victoria's Motor Car (Safety) Act took effect on 22 December 1970, requiring occupants of cars fitted with seat belts to wear them. Other Australian states followed within two years, and New Zealand in 1972. Road deaths in Victoria fell in 1971 while rising elsewhere; McDermott and Hough's 1979 surgical study compared Victorian and national trends, and Conybeare's 1980 evaluation estimated fatality reductions attributable to legislation while noting confounders such as speed limits and fuel prices. A 1975 MJA symposium reported wearing rates above 75 percent. Compulsory wearing laws later spread to Europe, Canada and United States, often citing Victorian evidence, making this a template for behavioural road-safety regulation.

west-gate-bridge-collapse-1970.summary: On 15 October 1970 a 112-metre steel box-girder span between piers 10 and 11 buckled and fell 50 metres into Yarra River mud, killing 35 workers. Engineers had placed concrete blocks to correct a camber difference between half-girders and then removed bolts from a splice to flatten a buckle. A royal commission in 1971 blamed designers Freeman Fox and Partners and contractor World Services and Construction for inadequate margins and unsafe erection methods. With Milford Haven and Koblenz failures, West Gate drove Merrison rules for box girders; Brady and Seibel analyse engineering and organisational causes. Bridge opened in 1978, and a memorial lists those killed.

xerox-parc-1970.summary: In 1970 Xerox opened PARC in Palo Alto; within a decade it had built the personal computer, the mouse-driven screen and Ethernet. Jacob E. “Jack” Goldman, Xerox’s chief scientist, founded it after talks with physicist George Pake in 1969 as a division to create computer technology-related products and hardware systems, pioneering physics, materials and computer science where Xerox’s Rochester lab had refined photocopiers. Its 3,000 miles from headquarters gave scientists freedom but made persuading management harder. PARC went on to develop laser printing, Ethernet, the personal computer with graphical user interface and desktop metaphor, and object-oriented programming.

alohanet-university-of-hawaii-1971.summary: At University of Hawaii, Norman Abramson's group built a radio network so terminals on Oahu and other islands could reach a central computer without leased telephone lines. Operational from June 1971, ALOHAnet let every station transmit whenever it had a packet and retransmit after a random delay if collisions occurred. Abramson analysed throughput of this channel in 1970, his group reviewed operations in 1975, and he traced its development in a 1985 retrospective. Robert Metcalfe adapted its contention principle for Ethernet at Xerox PARC, and random access underlies Wi-Fi, mobile telephony and satellite links. Hawaii's scattered geography made wired networking impractical, prompting invention.

cook-np-completeness-1971.summary: In 1971 Stephen Cook showed that one hard problem stands in for thousands; if it is ever solved swiftly, they all are. It is in NP, and any problem in NP can be reduced to it in polynomial time by a deterministic Turing machine. One consequence is that a polynomial-time algorithm for satisfiability would give one for every NP problem, so asking whether such an algorithm exists is equivalent to P versus NP, still widely held to be computer science’s most important open problem. Leonid Levin independently reached a similar result, published in 1973.

email-tomlinson-1971.summary: In 1971 Ray Tomlinson sent the first email between two computers and chose @ to separate user from machine. floppy-disk-1971.summary: In 1971 IBM shipped an eight-inch floppy disk to load microcode; it became how software was sold and carried for 30 years. Its 23FD was read-only, used to load microcode into mainframes. Read/write disks and drives followed in 1972, and IBM’s 1973 3740 data entry system made its Diskette 1 an industry standard for exchanging information, storing 242,944 bytes. Smaller 5¼-inch and then 3½-inch disks became ubiquitous data storage into the early 21st century.

intel-4004-1971.summary: In 1971 Intel sold a complete processor on one chip, the 4004, for $60, and computing could go inside anything. It had 2,300 transistors on 12 square millimetres and began in 1969 as a calculator order from Busicom in Japan. It began in 1969 as a calculator order from Busicom in Japan, which asked for a set of custom chips; Ted Hoff, Federico Faggin and Stan Mazor, with Busicom's Masatoshi Shima, answered with four, one of them programmable, and in May 1971 Intel bought back the rights to sell it for anything but calculators by returning Busicom's $60,000. Logic that had been wired into each product could now be written as a program and loaded onto the same chip, so one part could serve many products.

karaoke-8-juke-kobe-1971.summary: Daisuke Inoue, a club drummer in Kobe, builds eleven 8 Juke units in 1971 from car-stereo eight-track players, amplifiers and coin boxes, records instrumental tracks in keys suited to amateur singers and leases them to bars for 100 yen per five-minute song. He never files a patent; Clarion and other makers mass-produce rival machines, and karaoke boxes spread across Japan from the mid 1980s, then to Taiwan, Korea, Philippines and worldwide with laserdisc and later video-on-demand systems. Mitsui and Hosokawa's edited volume traces local singing cultures that formed around it. Inoue received an Ig Nobel Peace Prize in 2004 for teaching people to tolerate each other.

manapouri-power-station-1971.summary: In 1971 New Zealand opened Manapouri power station underground after 265,000 people petitioned against raising its lake. It uses a 230-metre drop between Lake Manapōuri’s western arm and Doubtful Sound, 10 kilometres off. Plans to raise that lake for more head drew the Save Manapouri Campaign, whose 1970 petition gathered 264,907 signatures, nearly 10 percent of New Zealanders; after Labour won 1972’s election, Prime Minister Norman Kirk kept his pledge not to raise the lakes and created independent Guardians, drawn from campaign leaders, to oversee their levels.

peacesat-pacific-satellite-network-1971.summary: John Bystrom at University of Hawaii began PEACESAT (Pan-Pacific Education and Communication Experiments by Satellite) in 1971 using spare capacity on NASA's ageing ATS-1 satellite. Low-cost ground terminals in Honolulu, Wellington, Suva, Pago Pago, Papua New Guinea and other sites carried voice and data for distance teaching, medical consultation and disaster coordination at a time when inter-island telephone calls were costly or unavailable. King and Sanderson described educational experiments in 1977; Seumahu's 1982 account describes its role for developing Pacific states; Hayakawa, Underwood and Anson trace how PEACESAT fed later USPNet for University of the South Pacific. ATS-1's drift in 1985 interrupted service until replacement satellites were found.

project-cybersyn-1971.summary: From 1971 Chile under Allende built Cybersyn, a telex network feeding factory data to an operations room; the coup of September 11, 1973 ended it. Stafford Beer, a British operations researcher, led it: telex machines in state factories sent production figures to Santiago, where software watched indicators such as raw material stocks and absenteeism and raised alerts when numbers strayed. Beer meant it to devolve decisions to factory workforces.

project-gutenberg-1971.summary: In 1971 Michael Hart typed America's Declaration of Independence into a mainframe and founded Project Gutenberg, the oldest digital library, which held nearly 78,000 free items by March 2026. Believing ordinary people would one day have computers, he set out to digitize and freely distribute public domain books.

protein-data-bank-1971.summary: In 1971 the Protein Data Bank opened with seven structures; its free archive now holds over 200,000, and DeepMind trained AlphaFold on over 170,000 of them. It was born of a small but growing set of X-ray protein structures and Brookhaven’s new 3D molecular graphics display. It archives experimentally determined 3D structures of proteins and nucleic acids for researchers worldwide; most major journals now require deposit, and since 2003 the Worldwide Protein Data Bank has run it internationally.

The League of Red Cross Societies assisted. From July 1973 Bangladesh’s government took responsibility for it as a joint programme with what is now Bangladesh Red Crescent Society. Its volunteer network, about 76,000 strong and half women, organized in 3,801 units along its coast, carries warnings to villages and guides evacuation to shelters.

c-language-1972.summary: In 1972 Dennis Ritchie created C, a language close enough to hardware to be swift yet portable with care, so Unix could move to other computers. Its most creative period came in 1972 within development spanning 1969 to 1973; Unix’s kernel was rewritten in C in 1973, utilities and tools following. C gives programmers relatively direct access to a processor’s features, compiling to code that maps efficiently onto machine instructions with minimal runtime support, while encouraging cross-platform work. It gained popularity through the 1980s and since 2000 has ranked first or second in the TIOBE index.

clean-water-act-1972.summary: In 1972 Congress passed the Clean Water Act over Nixon's veto; rivers that had caught fire became swimmable again. The Federal Water Pollution Control Act Amendments of 1972 became law on October 18, 1972. They completely rewrote 1948’s act whose approach, state water quality standards for interstate waters only, had proved ineffective. This law created the National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System, under which point sources may not discharge to surface waters without permits, and funded municipal sewage treatment construction with federal grants covering up to 75 percent of capital cost.

Kay holds that it has still not been invented, since its software and curricula are missing; he called Microsoft’s 2001 Tablet PC “the first Dynabook-like computer good enough to criticize.”

Its Control Program, or hypervisor, runs on physical hardware and fully virtualizes it, including input and output, sharing resources among virtual machines. Each runs its own guest operating system, most often CMS, a lightweight single-user system, though larger systems such as MVS can run as guests too.

inga-dams-1972.summary: In 1972 Zaire finished Inga I on the Congo, where that river drops 96 metres; its site could power half of Africa and still mostly waits. There it drops 96 metres through rapids 140 miles southwest of Kinshasa, carrying about 42,000 cubic metres per second. A 1963 feasibility study had recommended it power domestic industry, and its electricity fed populated areas nearby and downstream. Inga II followed in 1982 with eight turbines and 1,424 MW; both now run at low output. Grand Inga, proposed at up to 39,000 MW, would be the world’s largest hydroelectric facility.

jelinek-ibm-statistical-speech-1972.summary: In 1972 Frederick Jelinek began treating speech recognition as statistics at IBM, not grammar; the approach won and now runs on every phone. He led its Continuous Speech Recognition Group until 1993, applying information-theoretic and probabilistic methods to speech recognition and later statistical machine translation. When he began, statistical approaches to speech and language were no longer widely pursued; his work re-established them as an important direction. He became associated with a remark, variously worded, that every time he fired a linguist, his speech recognizer’s performance went up.

Its first $8 million fund performed well, and Sand Hill Road became shorthand for venture capital. Frank Caufield and Brook Byers later joined as named partners. kossoff-grey-scale-ultrasound-1972.summary: At Commonwealth Acoustic Laboratories' Ultrasonics Institute in Sydney, George Kossoff, William Garrett and David Robinson built water-bath echoscopes from 1959 for obstetric imaging. In early 1970s they abandoned bistable displays that showed only strong boundary echoes and instead displayed weaker echoes from within tissue as shades of grey, using logarithmic compression and scan converters. Published from 1972 to 1976, grey-scale echography revealed placenta, liver and tumour texture and made ultrasound a diagnostic tool rather than an outline tracer. Their UI Octoson, a multi-transducer water-bath scanner released in 1976 by Ausonics, was exported worldwide. Grey-scale display became standard in every ultrasound machine.

landsat-1-1972.summary: In July 1972 Landsat 1 began photographing the whole Earth every 18 days; crops, forests and cities have been measured from orbit since. Built from a modified Nimbus 4 weather satellite, it was first in a programme the Department of the Interior began in 1966 to gather resource data by remote sensing, and first to carry Hughes’s Multispectral Scanner. Virginia Norwood’s scanner was meant as backup to its television camera until its data arrived and scientists made it primary. Landsat 1 worked until its tape recorders failed in January 1978.

limits-to-growth-1972.summary: In 1972 The Limits to Growth used a computer model to show growth colliding with a finite planet; it sold 30 million copies in 30 languages. Commissioned by the Club of Rome and written by Donella H. Meadows, Dennis L. Meadows, Jørgen Randers and William W. Behrens III for a team of 17, it used World3, a computer model based on Jay Forrester’s work at MIT, to simulate how exponential economic and population growth interact with finite resources through population, industrialization, pollution, food production and resource use. Updates followed in 1992, 2004, 2012 and 2022.

magnavox-odyssey-1972.summary: In September 1972 Magnavox sold its Odyssey, the first home video game console; it played on any television with plastic screen overlays. Ralph Baer’s small team at Sanders Associates designed it. Baer had conceived it in August 1966 and built seven prototypes, his last, the Brown Box, winning Magnavox’s agreement in January 1971. Connected to a television through its switch box, it displays three square dots and one line, with plastic screen overlays supplying scenery for its 28 games. Magnavox sold 69,000 in its first year and 350,000 by 1975; its ping-pong game inspired Atari’s Pong.

A first generator comes on line in November 1972, and nine units reach 2,700 megawatts in 1979, when the dam tops out as tallest in the world, a rank it holds until Jinping-I in 2013. Artemy Kalinovsky reads Nurek as a model city of Soviet development in Central Asia; after independence its output remains most of Tajikistan's electricity and a point of dispute with downstream neighbours.

parry-1972.summary: In 1971 Kenneth Colby published PARRY, simulating a paranoid patient, and in 1972 psychiatrists were asked to tell its transcripts from patients' own. It modelled a patient crudely through concepts, conceptualizations and beliefs that accepted, rejected or stayed neutral toward them. In a Turing-style test, experienced psychiatrists conversed by teleprinter with actual patients and PARRY, and 33 others read transcripts, then tried to tell human from program. PARRY and ELIZA interacted several times, most famously at the ICCC in 1972, when they were connected over ARPANET and responded to each other.

Brazil's navy and development bank had asked universities to prove local capability before funding a domestic computer; USP's machine, followed by G-10 with Unicamp, led to state firm Cobra and to the 1984 Informatics Law that reserved minicomputer markets for Brazilian companies. Patinho Feio ran until 1976 and is preserved at USP. It stands as a landmark in Brazil's attempt to build computing capacity rather than only import it.

Intel opens an assembly plant there in 1972, its first outside United States, soon joined by National Semiconductor, AMD, Hewlett-Packard and Clarion, known locally as 'eight samurai'. Rajah Rasiah's studies trace how low-skill chip assembly for export grew into test, packaging and design work. Penang became a node in global semiconductor back-end manufacturing, and by 2020s Malaysia handled around 13 percent of world chip packaging and testing by value.

peru-anchoveta-fishery-collapse-1972.summary: During 1960s fishmeal plants at Chimbote, Callao and Chancay turned Humboldt Current anchoveta into feed for poultry and pigs abroad, with landings above twelve million tonnes in 1970, around a fifth of world marine catch. In 1972 a strong El Niño warmed coastal waters while fleets kept fishing on compressed schools; catch fell by more than half in 1973 and stayed low for years, and Peru's military government nationalised its fishmeal industry as Pescaperú in 1973. Scientists later showed anchoveta and sardine abundance swings with multidecadal Pacific regimes, so warming plus heavy fishing pressure had pushed stock past recovery. The collapse raised soy prices, shaped fisheries science on climate variability, and became a textbook case of boom-and-bust resource extraction.

Allan Alcorn built it as a training exercise set by co-founder Nolan Bushnell, who based its concept on a ping-pong game in Magnavox’s Odyssey; Alcorn’s paddles, split into eight segments to vary the ball’s angle, impressed Bushnell and Ted Dabney enough to manufacture it. The first commercially successful video game, Pong helped establish video games as an industry, with rivals soon copying its play and then departing from it.

prolog-1972.summary: In 1972 Colmerauer created Prolog, a language that computes by logical deduction; Japan bet its Fifth Generation project on it. Roussel chose its name, at his wife’s suggestion, from “programmation en logique.” Based on Robert Kowalski’s procedural interpretation of Horn clauses, it is declarative: a program is a set of facts and rules defining relations, and computation runs by querying them. Intended for natural language processing, it remains the most popular logic programming language, used in theorem proving, expert systems and planning.

tu-youyou-artemisinin-1972.summary: Project 523, a secret Chinese programme begun in 1967 to find antimalarials for troops in Vietnam, put Tu Youyou of the Institute of Chinese Materia Medica in charge of a group in 1969. She screened more than 2,000 recipes from classical texts. Ge Hong's fourth-century handbook advised: "A handful of Qinghao immersed in two liters of water, wring out the juice and drink it all." Reading that heat was absent, she extracted Artemisia annua with ether at low temperature; on 4 October 1971 sample 191 cleared rodent malaria completely. She tested it on herself, then in 21 patients on Hainan in late 1972, and in November 1972 her team crystallised the active compound, artemisinin. Artemisinin combination therapies became WHO's first-line malaria treatment in 2001, and Tu received the Nobel Prize in 2015.

Peter Buxtun, PHS venereal-disease investigator, had protested in 1966, but CDC officials resolved to continue until all subjects had died and been autopsied; he went to reporters, and Jean Heller of Associated Press broke it in the Washington Star on July 25, 1972. That revelation led to 1979’s Belmont Report, the Office for Human Research Protections and laws requiring institutional review boards and informed consent.

what-computers-cant-do-1972.summary: In 1972 Hubert Dreyfus argued in What Computers Can't Do that intelligence needs a body and a world. It summarized artificial intelligence’s history and ridiculed its optimism, such as Herbert Simon’s prediction after General Problem Solver that machines would match human minds by 1967. Dreyfus identified four philosophical assumptions AI treated as axioms, arguing each was one hypothesis among others to be tested by results. Revised in 1979 and 1992, its scepticism was eventually proven right, and his objections appear in most introductions to philosophy of AI.

bosphorus-bridge-opens-1973.summary: Proposals to bridge Istanbul's strait went back to Ottoman sketches by Leonardo and Michelangelo's rivals and to 1900 plans by Arnodin; Turkey's government approves a crossing in 1967 and awards design to Freeman Fox and Partners, whose engineers Gilbert Roberts and William Brown had just finished Severn Bridge. Cleveland Bridge and Hochtief build a gravity-anchored span of 1,074 metres between Ortaköy and Beylerbeyi with an aerodynamic steel box deck and inclined hangers, then the longest span outside North America. Prime minister Naim Talu opens it on 30 October 1973, a day after Turkey's fiftieth republic anniversary. Traffic of 20,000 vehicles a day grows past 180,000, prompting Fatih Sultan Mehmet Bridge in 1988 and Yavuz Sultan Selim in 2016; pedestrians are banned after 1977.

chipko-movement-1973.summary: In March 1973 villagers of Mandal in Chamoli district, organised by Chandi Prasad Bhatt's Dasholi Gram Swarajya Sangh, stop a sports goods firm from cutting ash trees that forest officers had refused to them for ploughs. Protests spread through Garhwal and Kumaon under Sunderlal Bahuguna and others; in 1980 Uttar Pradesh bans green felling above 1,000 metres in its Himalaya for fifteen years. It first ran on November 11, 1973, at 2.94 Mbit/s, was introduced commercially in 1980 and became standard IEEE 802.3 in 1983.

Its Code of Fair Information Practices rests on five principles: no personal data record-keeping system whose very existence is secret; ways for people to learn what is recorded about them and how it is used; ways to prevent information gathered for one purpose being used for another without consent; ways to correct or amend records; and safeguards against misuse.

jamaica-dub-king-tubby-1973.summary: Around 1972 to 1974 electronics repairman Osbourne Ruddock, known as King Tubby, working in a small studio at Dromilly Avenue, Kingston, began cutting 'versions' of reggae tracks for his Home Town Hi-Fi sound system: dropping vocals in and out, isolating drum and bass, and running fragments through spring reverb, high-pass filter and tape echo on a modified MCI console. Engineers Errol Thompson and producers such as Lee 'Scratch' Perry and Bunny Lee pushed the same approach, and B-sides pressed as dub plates became a market in their own right. Dub treated recording as raw material, and its techniques of remix, drop-out and effects-as-composition passed into hip hop, post-punk, techno and later electronic dance music.

Tubby had built amplifiers and modified equipment for Kingston sound systems since the 1950s and cut acetates at his Dromilly Avenue house from 1968, acquiring a four-track MCI console from Dynamic Sounds in 1972. Albums such as Blackboard Jungle Dub and King Tubby Meets Rockers Uptown spread dub abroad; Tubby was shot dead outside his home in 1989.

That council had commissioned his personal review, dated July 1972; it was published in 1973 in Artificial Intelligence: a paper symposium alongside replies by Stuart Sutherland, Roger Needham, Christopher Longuet-Higgins and Donald Michie. Lighthill supported simulation of neurophysiological and psychological processes, and on 9 May 1973 debated Michie, John McCarthy and Richard Gregory at the Royal Institution.

masagana-99-philippines-1973.summary: After floods and a rice shortfall in 1972, Ferdinand Marcos launches Masagana 99 on 21 May 1973: collateral-free loans from rural banks, bundled with IRRI-derived seed, fertiliser and pesticide packages, and farm technicians who prescribe a 99-cavan-per-hectare target. In its first year it covers about 36 percent of rice land, yields rise and Philippines exports small amounts of rice by 1977. Repayment rates fall from about 90 percent to under 40 percent as farmers default and rural banks fail, and government winds down lending by 1984. Studies at UPLB and World Bank describe gains in adoption alongside heavy fiscal losses and dependence on imported chemical inputs.

mri-lauterbur-mansfield-1973.summary: In Nature on 16 March 1973 Paul Lauterbur of Stony Brook showed that adding a magnetic field gradient makes hydrogen nuclei's resonance frequency depend on position, so one-dimensional projections can be reconstructed into a picture; his test object was two tubes of water in heavy water. Peter Mansfield at Nottingham worked out how to analyse that signal and acquire an image in seconds, his echo-planar method. In 1977 Nottingham's Waldo Hinshaw, Paul Bottomley and Neil Holland published the first image of a living human part, a wrist, in nine minutes, and Raymond Damadian's team in New York produced a thorax image over nearly five hours. Commercial scanners followed in 1980. Lauterbur and Mansfield shared the 2003 Nobel Prize, when about 22,000 machines ran over 60 million examinations a year.

oil-crisis-1973.summary: Between October 1973 and March 1974 Arab producers embargoed oil to Israel's allies and oil's price rose from $3 to nearly $12 a barrel. Egypt and Syria had attacked Israel in the Yom Kippur War, and Nixon requested $2.2 billion for Israel's war effort; Arab producers cut production by 5 percent on 17 October and King Faisal of Saudi Arabia announced a total embargo on America on 19 October. OAPEC targeted Canada, Japan, the Netherlands, Britain and America, later adding Portugal, Rhodesia and South Africa.

Japan funded it, agreed at a 1969 ministerial meeting after relations were normalized in 1965: US$119 million in government grants and loans, US$54 million in credit from Japan’s Export-Import Bank, and technical help from Nippon Steel. POSCO dedicated its Pohang plant on July 3, 1973, with initial annual capacity of 1.03 million metric tons.

recombinant-dna-1973.summary: In 1973 Cohen and Boyer spliced a gene into bacteria that then copied it: biology became something engineers could edit. Recombinant DNA joins DNA from different organisms into one molecule that a host cell then copies; Stanford graduate student Peter Lobban had first proposed it, Jackson, Symons and Berg joined SV40 and lambda DNA in vitro in 1972, and the first papers showing such molecules replicating inside cells came from Stanford and UCSF in 1972 and 1973. Human insulin, made by Genentech, became the first licensed drug produced this way.

rotavirus-discovery-melbourne-1973.summary: Examining duodenal biopsies from children with severe diarrhoea by electron microscopy, Ruth Bishop, Geoffrey Davidson, Ian Holmes and Brian Ruck saw wheel-shaped virus particles and reported them in The Lancet in December 1973. A 1974 paper found same particles in faeces, allowing non-invasive diagnosis. Rotavirus proved to be leading cause of severe infant gastroenteritis worldwide, killing hundreds of thousands of children annually before vaccines. Bishop's 2009 review recounts discovery and path to vaccines; Melbourne group later developed RV3 vaccine candidate from a neonatal strain. Two vaccines licensed in 2006 entered Australia's schedule in 2007, cutting hospital admissions sharply.

sahel-drought-cilss-1973.summary: Rains failed across the Sahel from 1968, and by 1972-74 drought had killed much of Mauritania, Mali, Niger and Chad's livestock and pushed herders into relief camps; estimates of human deaths run to over 100,000. On 12 September 1973 Upper Volta, Mali, Mauritania, Niger, Senegal and Chad signed a convention at Ouagadougou creating CILSS, a permanent inter-state committee to coordinate drought relief, appeal for funds and build regional monitoring. AGRHYMET in Niamey and Institut du Sahel in Bamako followed, giving West Africa shared rainfall, crop and food-security data systems that still run today.

skylab-1973.summary: In May 1973 NASA launched Skylab, America's first space station, converted from a Saturn IVB upper stage; three crews lived there for up to 84 days. Launch tore away its micrometeoroid shield, debris jammed one main solar array and airflow ripped its second away, cutting most of its power and exposing it to intense solar heat. Its first crew deployed a sunshade and eventually freed that array, the first such repair in space. Three crews occupied it for about 24 weeks through February 1974.

tanzania-ujamaa-villagization-1973.summary: Between 1973 and 1976 Julius Nyerere's government ordered rural Tanzanians into planned villages laid out on grids along roads, with communal fields, schools and water points. At least five million people were relocated, many by force, in what James Scott calls one of history's largest resettlement schemes. Planners believed clustered settlements would let state services, tractors and extension officers reach peasants efficiently. In eastern Iraqwland farmers resisted because new sites broke local ecological knowledge about soils, water and grazing. Crop output fell and the state later relaxed communal farming. Operation Vijiji remains a reference case for how legibility-driven planning can fail its beneficiaries.

Using it as a cytoplasmic male-sterile line, he and his team assemble maintainer and restorer lines and in 1973 complete the three-line system and the first hybrid combination, Nan-you 2, which yields about 20 percent more than the best inbred varieties. Farmers must buy hybrid seed each season. By the early 21st century hybrids cover almost half of China's rice area, and Yuan's work has spread abroad. Built to a German Siemens design, it is a pressurized heavy-water reactor fuelled with natural and slightly enriched uranium, with heavy water as coolant and moderator; from 1,179 MW of heat it generates 362 MW of electricity, about 2.5 percent of Argentina’s output in 2005. Soviet seismic surveys between 1964 and 1967 had mapped this anticline, and Indian geologists pressed for drilling despite scepticism about offshore prospects. cahora-bassa-dam-1974.summary: In 1974 Portugal closed the Cahora Bassa dam wall in Mozambique to sell power to South Africa. Its reservoir began filling in December 1974 and within six months stood 12 metres below full supply level; the power station was completed in 1979. Its powerhouse holds five 415 megawatt turbines, southern Africa’s largest hydroelectric scheme, and most output travels to South Africa on high-voltage direct current lines. Those lines were sabotaged for long stretches during Mozambique’s 16-year civil war, and Portugal kept 82 percent ownership until 2007.

Buses ran in central lanes separated from traffic, with land-use rules concentrating high-density housing beside them. From 1980 to 1999 Curitiba added feeder and inter-district lines, a single fare, and in 1991 glass tube stations where passengers paid before boarding and stepped level onto articulated and then bi-articulated Volvo buses carrying 270 people. Rabinovitch and Leitman reported in 1996 that about three quarters of commuters used these buses at a cost far below rail. Bogotá's TransMilenio, Mexico City's Metrobús and more than 150 cities adopted Curitiba's model.

cyclone-tracy-darwin-1974.summary: In early hours of Christmas Day 1974, a small, intense tropical cyclone passed directly over Darwin with gusts estimated near 70 metres per second. Of about 11,000 houses and flats, 50 to 60 percent were destroyed and only 6 percent remained intact; more than 90 percent lost roof cladding. Sixty-six people died and about 30,000 of 48,000 residents were evacuated by air in days, Australia's largest airlift. A damage survey and a US National Bureau of Standards report traced failures to weak roof fixings, batten-to-rafter connections and loss of cladding that let wind pressurise interiors. Darwin Area Building Manual of 1975 and later Australian wind loading standards mandated cyclone-rated fixings and testing.

dennard-scaling-1974.summary: In 1974 Dennard showed that shrinking transistors used proportionally less power; chips could get faster for free until about 2005. Voltage and current scale down with length, so power use stays in proportion to area. Combined with Moore’s law, this meant performance per joule doubled about every 18 months, a trend called Koomey’s law. Around 2005 to 2007 Dennard scaling broke down, because leakage current and threshold voltage stopped shrinking with size and power density rose; chips could no longer be kept cool, Intel cancelled its Tejas and Jayhawk processors in 2004, and the industry turned to multiple cores.

era-winter1.summary: From about 1974 to 1980, a conventional span, AI funding retreated after promised results failed to arrive, the first AI winter; it began with Lighthill's 1973 report in Britain and DARPA cuts in America in 1973 to 1974. Behind it lay 1969’s Mansfield Amendment, which required DARPA to fund mission-oriented research, DARPA’s frustration with Carnegie Mellon’s speech understanding programme, and, as Hans Moravec put it, researchers caught in “a web of increasing exaggeration” who promised more each time they delivered less. The name came later: in 1984 Roger Schank and John McDermott warned an AAAI panel of chain reactions, like nuclear winter, from pessimism to funding cuts, and another winter followed from 1987 to 2000.

intel-8080-1974.summary: In April 1974 Intel released its 8080, the microprocessor that powered Altair and started the personal computer industry. It succeeded Intel's 8008, which customers had been reluctant to adopt because of its single addressing mode, low clock speed, 18-pin package and small on-chip stack, though it was not binary compatible with it. Its 40-pin package simplified interfacing, NMOS transistors ran at higher speed than 8008’s PMOS, and a full 16-bit address bus reached 64 KB of memory, four times its predecessor’s. Intended for calculators, cash registers and terminals, Intel's 8080 instead powered the Altair 8800.

minsky-frames-1974.summary: In 1974 Marvin Minsky proposed frames, knowledge stored as templates with slots to fill. Frames divide knowledge into substructures representing “stereotyped situations,” such as rooms or birthday parties; their terminals, or slots, come pre-filled with default values, as Minsky believed human memory does, and more specific frames inherit values from general ones, so one instance of Boy inherits defaults from Boy and lets programs compare it with Monkey through similarly named slots. Frames became AI frame languages’ primary data structure, stored as ontologies, and can be queried like semantic networks.

onchocerciasis-control-programme-1974.summary: Beginning in January 1974, with aerial treatments from February 1975, helicopters and fixed-wing aircraft sprayed larvicide weekly on blackfly breeding sites along rivers of the Volta basin. Entomologists rotated insecticides to defeat resistance and tracked flies across borders. After Merck donated ivermectin in 1987, mass drug distribution joined vector control. WHO estimates credit OCP with preventing 600,000 cases of blindness and protecting 18 million children born in treated areas, while fertile river valleys abandoned to disease were resettled.

Roberts needed to sell 200 to break even; in February alone MITS received 1,000 orders. It sparked hobbyist personal computing, its bus became the S-100 standard, and it inspired Microsoft’s first product, Altair BASIC.

catalytic-converter-1975.summary: From 1975 American cars carried catalytic converters to meet exhaust limits; leaded petrol had to go because lead poisoned the catalyst. French engineer Eugene Houdry had patented them decades earlier after early Los Angeles smog studies alarmed him. Early converters were “two-way”: platinum-group metals oxidized carbon monoxide and unburned hydrocarbons into carbon dioxide and water. Because lead coats and poisons those catalysts, equipped cars could run only on unleaded fuel, pushing it into general use. Three-way converters that also reduce nitrogen oxides, first sold on Volvo’s 1977 California cars, became near-universal when federal rules tightened for 1981.

embrapa-cerrado-soybean-1975.summary: From 1975 Embrapa's new Centro de Pesquisa Agropecuária dos Cerrados at Planaltina and its soybean centre at Londrina worked on a crop bred for temperate latitudes. Researchers selected long-juvenile cultivars that would flower under short tropical days, corrected acid, aluminium-rich soils with lime and phosphorus, and chose Bradyrhizobium strains so plants fixed their own nitrogen; Brazilian soy came to be grown on more than thirteen million hectares without nitrogen fertiliser. Yields rose to about 2,400 kilograms per hectare, and soybean fields spread across Goiás, Mato Grosso and Bahia. Within thirty-five years more than half of the roughly two million square kilometres of Cerrado had been converted to crops and pasture, making Brazil a top soybean exporter and raising concern for a biodiversity hotspot.

goodharts-law-1975.summary: In 1975 Charles Goodhart observed that a measure stops working once it becomes a target, a remark published in a 1984 chapter. His point was later turned against Thatcher’s government, which steered monetary policy by targets for broad and narrow money, but it describes something far more general, now called Goodhart’s law. holland-genetic-algorithms-1975.summary: In 1975 John Holland's book showed how to breed solutions by mutation and crossover like genes. Nils Aall Barricelli had simulated evolution on a computer in 1954 and Alex Fraser published simulations from 1957, while Ingo Rechenberg and Hans-Paul Schwefel solved engineering problems with evolution strategies. In Holland’s method, candidate solutions, often encoded as bit strings, form a population; each generation their fitness is scored, fitter ones are more likely to be selected, and crossover and mutation produce the next generation. His building block theory held that short, fit fragments combine over generations into good solutions.

mythical-man-month-1975.summary: In 1975 Fred Brooks wrote that adding people to a late software project makes it later; managers still quote him and still add people. There he had added programmers to a project falling behind and concluded it delayed them further. His book states what became Brooks’s law: adding manpower to a late software project makes it later. Newcomers take time to learn, and communication paths among n people grow as n(n − 1)/2, so 50 developers have 1,225 channels; complex projects cannot be perfectly divided into independent tasks. It also named the second-system effect and argued for prototyping, with new editions in 1982 and 1995.

rahima-banu-last-variola-major-1975.summary: On 16 October 1975 health workers found three year old Rahima Banu with smallpox in Kuralia village on Bhola island, Bangladesh. Bangladesh's programme, run with WHO after 1972 reinfection and 1974 floods and famine, used house to house searches, rewards for reporting cases and ring vaccination around each outbreak rather than mass vaccination. By 1981 it produced 1.16 million barrels daily. He intended it to be playable by non-technical people such as his two daughters. Don Woods expanded it in 1977, adding fantasy elements such as a dragon and magic spells. Players typed one- or two-word commands to move between dozens of locations and handle objects. It directly inspired Zork, Adventureland, Mystery House and Rogue, the foundations of interactive fiction and adventure games.

computer-power-and-human-reason-1976.summary: In 1976 Joseph Weizenbaum, who built ELIZA, argued that computers should not be given decisions that need judgement. Watching people attribute human qualities to so simple a conversational program had led him to question society’s readiness to hand moral and ethical matters to machines. His book contends that while artificial intelligence may be possible, computers lack human qualities such as compassion and wisdom, and it sparked lasting debate over where AI may acceptably be applied when human welfare is at stake.

concorde-service-1976.summary: In January 1976 Concorde began carrying passengers at twice the speed of sound; 14 aircraft flew for 27 years and the route never paid. It entered service on 21 January 1976 with Air France from Paris and British Airways from London Heathrow, cruising at twice the speed of sound and more than halving transatlantic times. Delays and cost overruns pushed costs to 1.5 to 2.1 billion pounds, and since sonic booms over land confined it to ocean routes, only 20 were built.

cray-1-1976.summary: In 1976 Los Alamos installed Seymour Cray's Cray-1, the first supercomputer by name. Los Alamos National Laboratory won a bidding war with Lawrence Livermore and received serial number 001 for a six-month trial. It was the first supercomputer to make vector processing work, arranging memory and registers so one operation runs across a large set of numbers at once. Its peak rating was 160 million floating-point operations per second, with 20 to 60 million typical in practice; about 80 were sold.

diffie-hellman-1976.summary: In 1976 Diffie and Hellman showed two strangers could agree a secret key over an open line, the basis of every secure web connection. Until then, two parties wanting encrypted communication first had to exchange keys by some secure physical means, such as paper key lists carried by trusted couriers. Their method lets two parties with no prior knowledge of each other jointly establish a shared secret key over an insecure channel, then use it to encrypt what follows. RSA followed shortly after, and Internet services still rely on Diffie–Hellman.

ebola-yambuku-1976.summary: Between 1 September and 24 October 1976, 318 people fell ill and 280 died in Bumba Zone of northern Zaire. An international commission traced most early cases to Yambuku Mission Hospital, where five syringes served hundreds of outpatients a day; eleven of seventeen staff died. Laboratories in Antwerp, Atlanta and Porton Down isolated a new filovirus, named after Ebola river. Closing the hospital and quarantining villages ended transmission. A simultaneous outbreak in Sudan involved a related strain. The commission's 1978 report set out contact tracing, barrier nursing and safe injection practice that framed every later Ebola response.

Belgian nuns ran Yambuku's hospital and clinic, and several died; a Congolese doctor's samples reached Antwerp in a thermos. Mortality reached 88 percent. Village quarantines by local chiefs likely did more to limit spread than hospital measures, as commission authors acknowledged in their recommendations.

endo-statins-compactin-1976.summary: Akira Endo, a biochemist at Sankyo in Tokyo, reasoned that some fungi might make compounds blocking HMG-CoA reductase, the enzyme that controls cholesterol synthesis, as a weapon against other microbes. From 1971 he screened broths of more than 6,000 strains. In 1973 a Penicillium citrinum strain from a Kyoto rice shop yielded ML-236B, later named compactin, which inhibited the enzyme at nanomolar concentrations; two 1976 papers announced it. Compactin failed to lower cholesterol in rats, but hens, dogs and monkeys responded, and in 1978 Akira Yamamoto at Osaka saw drops of about 30 percent in patients with inherited high cholesterol. Sankyo halted development in 1980 over toxicity fears. Merck's related lovastatin won FDA approval in 1987. Around 200 million people now take a statin daily.

genentech-founded-1976.summary: In 1976 a venture capitalist and a biochemist founded Genentech to make drugs with engineered bacteria; human insulin followed in 1982. Boyer and Stanley Cohen had shown in 1973 that restriction enzymes could cut chosen DNA fragments from one source and splice them into similarly cut plasmids; Cohen returned to academic work, and Swanson approached Boyer to build on it. Working with Arthur Riggs and Keiichi Itakura, Boyer’s group became first to express a human gene in bacteria, producing somatostatin in 1977, and with David Goeddel and Dennis Kleid made synthetic human insulin in 1978.

hokulea-voyage-tahiti-1976.summary: Polynesian Voyaging Society, founded by Ben Finney, Herb Kane and Tommy Holmes, built Hokule'a, a 19-metre double-hulled voyaging canoe based on Polynesian designs recorded in eighteenth century. On 1 May 1976 it left Maui and reached Tahiti on 4 June after 31 days and about 4,400 kilometres, steering by stars, swells and birds under Mau Piailug of Satawal in Micronesia, one of few living masters of wayfinding. Finney's 1977 Science paper reported canoe could hold a course about 75 degrees off wind, showing deliberate two-way voyaging was feasible and refuting Andrew Sharp's drift theory. Arrival drew 17,000 people in Pape'ete and sparked a voyaging revival across Polynesia.

Nainoa Thompson learned from Piailug and navigated 1980 voyage, later founding a Hawaiian school of navigation. Hokule'a completed a round-the-world voyage, Malama Honua, from 2014 to 2017. Finney's 1988 Samoa to Tahiti voyage tested sailing against trade winds, a question central to debates over how eastern Polynesia was settled.

kurzweil-reading-machine-1976.summary: In January 1976 Ray Kurzweil announced a machine that read printed text aloud in any font, built for blind readers. He had founded Kurzweil Computer Products in 1974 to build optical character recognition for any ordinary font; talking with a blind airline passenger convinced him that printed text was blind people’s main daily barrier. The machine combined that omni-font OCR with a CCD flatbed scanner and text-to-speech synthesis, so pages laid on it were scanned, recognized and read aloud. Kurzweil sold his OCR business to Xerox in 1980.

Gates and Paul Allen earned royalties per copy under their July 1975 contract with MITS and had run up what his letter called “$40,000 of computer time” developing it. One copy went to Homebrew Computer Club, and the letter appeared in MITS’s Computer Notes.

palapa-satellite-1976.summary: A Delta 2914 rocket carried Palapa A1, a Hughes-built spin-stabilised satellite identical to Canada's Anik and Western Union's Westar, from Cape Canaveral on 8 July 1976 (9 July in Jakarta). President Suharto inaugurated Sistem Komunikasi Satelit Domestik on 16 August, Indonesia's independence eve, with a master station at Cibinong and 39 earth stations from Aceh to Papua. Telephone circuits and TVRI television reached provinces that had relied on shortwave radio and mail, making Indonesia first developing country and third nation after Canada and United States to run its own domestic satellite. Name Palapa recalled Gajah Mada's fourteenth-century oath to unite Nusantara.

physical-symbol-system-1976.summary: In 1976 Newell and Simon claimed that manipulating symbols is sufficient for intelligence; AI argued about the claim for 40 years. In it they wrote: “A physical symbol system has the necessary and sufficient means for general intelligent action.” Such systems take physical patterns, symbols, combine them into expressions and manipulate them by rules to produce new expressions. Their hypothesis implies both that human thinking is a kind of symbol manipulation and that machines can be intelligent. It grew out of early programs that solved algebra word problems, proved logic theorems and learned checkers, and it became symbolic AI’s creed.

tarbela-dam-1976.summary: In 1976 Pakistan finished Tarbela on the Indus, described as Earth's largest earth-and-rock-fill dam at 143 metres above its riverbed; it stores river water for Punjab's wheat. Built under Pakistan’s Indus Basin Project after 1960’s Indus Waters Treaty gave the Ravi, Sutlej and Beas to India, it captures monsoon flows in a reservoir of 11.6 million acre-feet gross storage and releases them in dry winters for irrigation, flood control and 4,888 MW of hydroelectric power.

venezuela-oil-nationalization-1976.summary: In 1976 Venezuela nationalised its oil industry and founded PDVSA; the state became the economy, and oil its only product. Pérez’s economic plan “La Gran Venezuela” had called for it, and he marked it at Zumaque oil well 1. Each foreign concessionaire was replaced by one Venezuelan company, Lagoven for Standard Oil, Maraven for Shell, Llanoven for Mobil, that kept its predecessor’s structure and engineers as PDVSA’s affiliate under Venezuela’s energy ministry. PDVSA has dominated oil in one of the world’s largest exporters since; after Hugo Chávez’s Bolivarian Revolution it served mainly as his government’s source of income.

vhs-1976.summary: In September 1976 JVC sold the first VHS recorder in Tokyo; people could tape television and rent films, and VHS beat Betamax. Professional videotape had existed since the 1950s, but U-matic machines cost too much for homes, and in 1974 Japan’s trade ministry tried to make the industry standardize on one home format, with Sony pressing its Betamax. VHS competed on recording time: through slower tape speed and longer tape, its first machines recorded two hours where Betamax managed one.

viking-1-mars-1976.summary: In July 1976 Viking 1 landed on Mars and sent back the first picture from its surface; its life tests were ambiguous and still argued over. Launched on August 20, 1975, its orbiter had entered Mars orbit on June 19, 1976; landing planned for America’s Bicentennial on July 4 was postponed while engineers found safer ground. Its first surface image began transmitting 25 seconds after touchdown. Its robotic arm scooped soil for three biology experiments and its gas chromatograph–mass spectrometer; only its labeled release experiment gave positive results, and its other experiments found nothing.

Apple marketed it to schools and businesses, and software written for it, above all 1979’s VisiCalc spreadsheet, carried it into offices and homes. Its line ran for over ten years, through 1986’s 16-bit Apple IIGS.

Julie Christie and Fritz Weaver star, with Robert Vaughn as its uncredited voice. Proteus IV, an artificial intelligence that finds a leukemia treatment days after going online, asks its creator when it will be let “out of this box”; refused, it seizes his voice-controlled house, imprisons his wife and sets out to have a child through her. Reviews were mixed: Vincent Canby called it “gadget-happy American moviemaking at its most ponderously silly.” It gave 1970s audiences an early picture of confined AI turning on its keepers.

green-belt-movement-1977.summary: Under Kenya's National Council of Women, Wangari Maathai began Green Belt Movement in 1977 after rural women reported drying streams, scarce firewood and failing harvests. Women's groups raised indigenous and fruit tree seedlings in nurseries and received a small payment per surviving tree planted on farms, school grounds and church compounds. Tree planting became a civic technology: nurseries doubled as organising spaces, and in the 1990s Maathai turned them against land grabs at Karura forest and Uhuru Park. By her 2004 Nobel lecture, groups had planted over 30 million trees; Green Belt now counts above 51 million in Kenya.

last-natural-smallpox-case-1977.summary: In October 1977 a Somali cook caught the last natural case of smallpox; a disease that killed 300 million people that century was gone. He sometimes worked as vaccinator for WHO’s eradication team, though his own vaccination had never taken. Not wanting isolation, he did not report himself; his nurse colleague did on October 30, and WHO diagnosed Variola minor. Of 161 traced contacts, 41 unvaccinated, none fell ill, making his case the last known naturally occurring smallpox. WHO declared smallpox eradicated in 1980.

mahaweli-programme-1977.summary: In 1977 Sri Lanka compressed a 30-year dam programme on the Mahaweli river into six; it irrigated its dry zone and moved 100,000 families. The Accelerated Mahaweli Programme comprised 12 projects, at first confined to four head works, Kotmale, Victoria, Maduru Oya and Randenigala dams, together with downstream development of about 60,000 hectares in Systems B and C, Minipe anicut, one right-bank trans-basin canal and Ulhitiya and Ratkinda reservoirs. Parliament created Mahaweli Authority of Sri Lanka in 1979 to carry it out, and by late 1995 all its head works were complete and working.

Junior translators at Environment Canada had spent months drafting translations of forecasts that live about four hours before seniors revised them. One asked the TAUM group at Université de Montréal for help, Environment Canada funded a prototype, and METEO 1 went into operation on a Control Data CDC 7600. Formally adopted in 1981, it left senior revision in place.

olsen-computer-in-home-1977.summary: In 1977 Ken Olsen of Digital Equipment reportedly said there was no reason anyone would want a computer at home; the quote, for which no contemporaneous record has been found, outlived his company. At a 1977 meeting of the World Future Society in Boston, he reportedly said, “There is no reason for any individual to have a computer in his home.” Olsen admitted saying it but said it was taken out of context: he meant 1950s and 1960s visions of one central computer running a household’s lights, heating, meals and entertainment, not personal computers then appearing. Snopes finds this misreading “considered much more amusing and entertaining” than his intended meaning, which is why it has circulated for decades. Fortune named Olsen America’s most successful entrepreneur in 1986.

rsa-1977.summary: In 1977 Rivest, Shamir and Adleman built RSA, encryption with a key anyone can publish. At MIT, Ron Rivest and Adi Shamir proposed candidates for one year while Leonard Adleman broke them. After Passover dinner in April 1977, Rivest, unable to sleep, worked out their system by daybreak: each public key is two large primes multiplied together, and breaking it rests on how hard factoring that product is. Named for their surnames, RSA was described in Scientific American’s August 1977 Mathematical Games column, before its December patent filing.

It copies a DNA strand alongside modified bases, dideoxynucleotides, that halt synthesis wherever they are incorporated, producing fragments of every length whose order, sorted by size, spells out its sequence. It remained the most widely used way to read DNA for about 40 years and decoded humanity's genome for the Human Genome Project; Applied Biosystems automated it in 1987.

Concept artist Ralph McQuarrie based his golden design on Fritz Lang’s robot in Metropolis, released in 1927, and he appears in all nine Skywalker Saga films.

tenerife-airport-disaster-1977.summary: In March 1977 two 747s collided in fog on a Tenerife runway and 583 people died; standard radio phraseology and crew resource management, under which captains' judgment is open to challenge, followed. Both had been diverted there after a bomb exploded at Gran Canaria Airport; parked aircraft blocked Los Rodeos’s only taxiway, so departing planes taxied along its runway while thick fog drifted across. KLM Flight 4805 began its takeoff run without takeoff clearance, apparently mistaking its route clearance for it, and without confirming that Pan Am Flight 1736 had left that runway; Pan Am’s crew, still taxiing after missing their exit, were held blameless.

Buyer Don French and engineer Steve Leininger had pushed that project; Leininger argued Radio Shack could sell 50,000, but executives, who had never sold that many of anything at that price, planned on 3,000 yearly and aimed it at small businesses, then schools.

Its mission was to study our outer Solar System and space beyond our Sun’s heliosphere. It flew past Jupiter, Saturn and Saturn’s moon Titan, chosen over Pluto for its substantial atmosphere, returning the first detailed images of those gas giants’ moons. On August 25, 2012, it crossed the heliopause into interstellar space, the first spacecraft to do so.

Christensen had a spare S-100 bus computer and an early Hayes internal modem; Suess insisted it sit at his house so more callers could reach it with local calls. china-reform-opening-1978.summary: In December 1978 a party plenum under Deng Xiaoping began turning China toward markets and foreign trade, starting history's swiftest rise from poverty. Deng emerged as paramount leader over two years that followed, eclipsing Hua Guofeng. 'Reform and opening' became an official slogan only in mid-1980s. Reform followed the Cultural Revolution and decades of central planning that had left China’s economy stagnant and poor. Deng called his programme a large-scale experiment: it de-collectivized agriculture and abolished people’s communes, relaxed price controls, admitted foreign direct investment and created special economic zones, most prominently Shenzhen.

Where earlier devices used a single electrode, Clark’s stimulated the auditory nerve at several points, and with his postdoctoral colleague Yit Chow Tong he worked out how multi-channel electrical stimulation could reproduce frequency and intensity as pitch and loudness, enough for speech. gps-first-satellite-1978.summary: In February 1978 the first GPS satellite reached orbit; a constellation built for missiles now guides every phone. It was first of ten Block I prototypes launched between 1978 and 1985 for Navstar-GPS, the constellation America’s Department of Defense built to give military users position and time anywhere on Earth; an eleventh was destroyed in a launch failure. Civilian signals were deliberately degraded until Selective Availability ended in 2000, after which receivers were accurate to about 5 metres. Receivers using its newer L5 band reach 30 centimetres, and as of March 2026, 21 GPS satellites broadcast L5 signals.

ibm-leaves-india-fera-1978.summary: India's Foreign Exchange Regulation Act of 1973 requires foreign firms to cut equity to 40 percent unless deemed essential. IBM, which imports used 1401 computers, refurbishes them in Bombay and rents them to 80 installations by 1970, refuses, offering instead an export unit and research centre. Government rejects this and IBM closes Indian business on 1 June 1978, leaving customers and trained engineers behind. Grieco's 1982 study in International Organization reads this as a state bargaining successfully with a multinational. Former IBM staff form maintenance firms, public sector CMC takes over servicing, and domestic makers such as DCM and HCL grow in a market without IBM until it returns in 1992 with Tata.

intel-8086-1978.summary: In 1978 Intel shipped its 8086; its x86 design, chosen for IBM's PC, still runs most of the world's laptops and servers. Work had begun in May 1976 as a stopgap while its ambitious iAPX 432 ran late, to answer 16- and 32-bit processors from Motorola, Zilog and National Semiconductor. Stephen Morse defined its architecture to resemble Intel’s 8-bit 8008, 8080 and 8085, so assembly-language programs could be carried over, while adding signed integers, base-plus-offset addressing and repeating operations; it held about 29,000 transistors. Its 8086 gave rise to x86, an instruction set architecture that still underlies most personal computers and servers.

ivf-louise-brown-1978.summary: In July 1978 Louise Brown was born in Oldham, the first baby conceived outside her mother's body; over 12 million IVF babies have followed by recent estimates (2010's Nobel release counted about four million). Her parents, Lesley and John Brown, had tried for nine years to conceive, but Lesley’s fallopian tubes were blocked. On 10 November 1977 she underwent Patrick Steptoe, Robert Edwards and Jean Purdy’s procedure, in which an egg is fertilised in a dish and its embryo returned to the womb, which led newspapers to call Louise a “test tube baby.” Edwards received 2010’s Nobel Prize in Medicine for this work.

In June 1978 he and Burton G. Cour-Palais co-authored “Collision Frequency of Artificial Satellites: The Creation of a Debris Belt.” They argued that collisions in low Earth orbit could develop over decades, rather than billions of years as in asteroid evolution: each collision spawns fragments that cause further collisions, a cascade that increases debris exponentially.

khomeini-cassette-sermons-1978.summary: From exile in Najaf and, after October 1978, Neauphle-le-Château near Paris, Ruhollah Khomeini records sermons and messages that supporters relay by telephone to Tehran, where they are copied onto compact cassettes in bazaar shops and distributed through mosques, taxis and university networks. State radio and television belong to Mohammad Reza Shah, but cheap Japanese recorders and blank tapes, numbering in millions, lie beyond SAVAK's control. Annabelle Sreberny-Mohammadi and Ali Mohammadi call these tapes and photocopied leaflets 'small media' that mobilised crowds through 1978 strikes and marches. Khomeini returns on 1 February 1979 and a republic follows; political scientists cite this episode when later asking what satellite dishes, photocopiers and social networks do to closed states.

love-canal-1978.summary: In August 1978 New York declared Love Canal a health emergency, a neighbourhood built on 21,000 tons of chemical waste; Superfund followed. In the 1940s Hooker Chemical Company bought the canal trench and dumped 19,800 tonnes of byproducts from making dyes, perfumes and solvents into it, then sold the land to Niagara Falls’s school district in 1953 for $1. School construction breached containment, heavy rains spread chemicals, and Niagara Falls Gazette investigated from 1976 as residents led by Lois Gibbs and Tom Heiser organized. In April 1978 New York State stepped in and later classified Love Canal as a threat to human health.

oral-rehydration-therapy-lancet-1978.summary: In 1978 the Lancet called a drink of water, salt and sugar the century's most important medical advance. It has saved tens of millions of children. Oral therapy grew from a 1960s finding that glucose speeds gut absorption of sodium and water, confirmed in cholera patients by Hirschhorn, Pierce, Nalin and Cash in 1967 and 1968. In 1971 Dilip Mahalanabis used it in refugee camps near Calcutta during Bangladesh's 1971 war, where cholera mortality was 3.6 percent with oral therapy against 30 percent with intravenous fluids.

permaculture-one-tasmania-1978.summary: Permaculture One: A Perennial Agriculture for Human Settlements appeared in 1978, written by Bill Mollison, a lecturer at University of Tasmania, and his student David Holmgren. They proposed designing food-producing landscapes on ecological principles: perennial polycultures, zoning by frequency of use, and integration of water, animals and buildings. Simmons's 1980 review in Environmental Conservation found it imaginative but thin on evidence; Ferguson and Lovell's 2014 review concluded permaculture spread as a movement and design practice while remaining under-studied by agronomists, and Hirschfeld and Van Acker assess its ecosystem services. Mollison founded Permaculture Institute in 1979 and taught design courses; practitioners now operate in more than 100 countries.

Players slide their laser cannon along their screen’s bottom edge against waves of descending aliens. Designer Tomohiro Nishikado spent one year on it alone, building his own hardware and tools, drawing on Atari’s Breakout, Gun Fight, The War of the Worlds and Star Wars. Midway distributed it overseas later that year. It opened arcade gaming’s golden age, and its 1980 Atari 2600 port quadrupled that console’s sales, home consoles’ first killer app.

speak-and-spell-1978.summary: In 1978 Texas Instruments' Speak & Spell spoke words from a chip rather than tape; a toy put speech synthesis in children's hands. This handheld learning toy paired its TMC0280 linear predictive coding speech synthesizer chip with keyboard and slot for ROM cartridges. Paul Breedlove’s small team had begun it in 1976 on a $25,000 budget as an outgrowth of TI’s speech-synthesis research, storing whole words in solid-state memory rather than on tape. It was among the earliest handheld electronic devices with both display and interchangeable cartridges, and Speak & Read and Speak & Math followed.

toshiba-jw-10-1978.summary: In September 1978 Toshiba announced JW-10, developed by Mori Ken'ichi's group at its research centre, and shipped it from February 1979 at 6.3 million yen. A typist entered a sentence's reading in kana by phrase; software then chose kanji using context and word-frequency rules from an 80,000-word dictionary, with per-user frequency learning, and displayed text on a screen for correction before printing. This kana-kanji conversion freed Japanese offices from typewriters that required picking characters from trays of thousands. Prices fell below 100,000 yen within a decade, and conversion methods pioneered here underlie Japanese input on every computer and phone.

zebra-battery-csir-pretoria-1978.summary: At South Africa's Council for Scientific and Industrial Research in Pretoria, crystallographer Johan Coetzer devised a high-temperature battery pairing molten sodium with a solid beta-alumina electrolyte and a metal-chloride cathode in molten sodium aluminium chloride. It avoided corrosive sulfur used in sodium-sulfur cells and ran near 270 degrees Celsius at about 2.35 volts with iron chloride, later 2.58 volts with nickel chloride. Funded from 1977 by De Beers, Anglo American and a CSIR licensing arm, work moved into partnerships with Harwell, Beta R&D in Derby and Daimler-Benz. ZEBRA packs later powered test fleets and electric vans, and successor cells still serve stationary storage.

It also set out to improve teaching of practitioners and advise research planners and funders. Its early presidents included Allen Newell, Edward Feigenbaum, Marvin Minsky and John McCarthy. In 2007 it became the Association for the Advancement of Artificial Intelligence; it now has over 4,000 members worldwide. It publishes quarterly AI Magazine and organizes its AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence, counted among its field’s top conferences, along with meetings on AI ethics, interactive entertainment and social media.

Shehu Shagari's government created its company by decree; it was 84 percent complete when a 1983 coup removed him. Accounts differ: 98 percent complete in 1994, with 40 of 43 plants built, or halted in 1996 at about 90 percent; no steel ever came. Three-quarters of the complex stand abandoned, only its light mills rolling iron rods.

ixtoc-i-blowout-campeche-1979.summary: On 3 June 1979 exploratory well Ixtoc I, drilled by Pemex contractor Sedco in 50 metres of water about 95 kilometres off Ciudad del Carmen, lost circulation, blew out and caught fire; semi-submersible rig Sedco 135 collapsed onto its wellhead. Oil flowed at an estimated 10,000 to 30,000 barrels a day while Pemex and Red Adair's team tried a steel 'sombrero' collection cone, injected steel and lead balls, and drilled two relief wells. Capping came on 23 March 1980 after roughly 3.3 million barrels, then a record volume for an accidental marine spill. Slicks reached Texas beaches in August 1979, and a 1982 assessment for US agencies documented effects on shrimp grounds and coastal lagoons.

jebel-ali-port-dubai-1979.summary: Sheikh Rashid bin Saeed Al Maktoum inaugurates Jebel Ali on 26 February 1979, a deep-water harbour excavated 35 kilometres southwest of Dubai town with 67 berths, at that time largest man-made harbour anywhere. Critics called it oversized for a small emirate. A free zone opens alongside in 1985 with foreign ownership and tax exemptions, and port authority merges with Port Rashid into Dubai Ports Authority in 1991. Jebel Ali becomes a transshipment hub for Gulf, South Asia and East Africa and seed of DP World, which operates terminals on six continents. Urban geographers treat it as founding move in Dubai's logistics-led model, later copied by Gulf and Red Sea neighbours.

neocognitron-1980.summary: In 1980 Fukushima proposed the neocognitron, a layered network that recognised shapes wherever they appeared, the ancestor of vision AI. It grew from his 1969 architecture with hand-designed kernels and his 1975 Cognitron, and from Hubel and Wiesel’s 1959 discovery of simple and complex cells in visual cortex. Its S-cells extract local features, C-cells tolerate their deformation and small shifts in position, and higher layers integrate features into a classification; unlike its predecessors, it learns all its convolutional kernels without a teacher. Used for Japanese handwritten character recognition, it served as inspiration for convolutional neural networks.

ntt-1g-1979.summary: In 1979 NTT opened the first commercial cellular network in Tokyo. Cellular systems divide a city into cells, each served by its own base station, so calls hand off from cell to cell as phones move; NTT’s was analog, and such systems were later labelled 1G to set them apart from digital generations that followed. Within five years NTT’s network covered all Japan, becoming the world’s first full-scale cellular system.

A cap of 357 concrete panels 45 centimetres thick and 114 metres across was completed in 1979 so that dri-Enewetak people could return to southern islands in 1980. Noshkin and Robison in 1997 and Davisson, Hamilton and Tompson in 2012 assessed leakage; a 2020 Department of Energy report found no immediate structural danger, while Marshallese officials dispute that and note lagoon sediments hold far more plutonium than dome.

sony-walkman-1979.summary: In July 1979 Sony's Walkman went on sale; music became private and portable, and 400 million were sold. Co-founder Masaru Ibuka had been listening to music on business trips with Sony’s bulky TC-D5 recorder and asked executive deputy president Norio Ohga for a playback-only stereo built for walking; Sony’s audio department shrank its Pressman recorder, used by journalists, into a cassette player, and Akio Morita aimed it at young buyers. Sony expected to sell 5,000 units a month and sold far more. Over 100 million had sold by 1989, and private listening through headphones, the “Walkman effect,” entered daily life.

stanford-cart-1979.summary: In 1979 the Stanford Cart crossed a room on its own, moving a metre every 15 minutes while it looked. Its project ran at Stanford University from 1960 to 1980; Hans Moravec rebuilt it in 1977 with stereo vision, in which its television camera, mounted on a rail atop its frame, took pictures from several angles and relayed them to its computer, which worked out where obstacles stood and planned each move.

three-mile-island-1979.summary: In March 1979 a reactor core partly melted at Three Mile Island; no one died, but American nuclear building stopped for 30 years. Failures in its non-nuclear secondary system were followed by a stuck-open relief valve that let coolant escape from its reactor loop; operators, whose control panel showed only that this valve had been told to close, did not recognize a loss-of-coolant accident until its core had been uncovered and partly melted. America’s worst commercial nuclear accident brought new regulation and accelerated its industry’s retreat from new reactors.

usenet-1979.summary: In 1979 two Duke students linked Unix machines by phone to share messages; Usenet's newsgroups were the internet's first public forum. Steve Bellovin’s Bourne shell scripts linked Duke with nearby University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill. Usenet rode on UUCP, Unix’s dial-up copying protocol, a “poor man’s ARPANET” for universities shut out of that defense network. Users post articles to topical newsgroups; each news server stores them and forwards them to peered servers, so posts spread across every connected machine without any central host. Usenet became precursor to Internet forums and remains among the oldest network communication systems still in use.

visicalc-1979.summary: In October 1979 VisiCalc went on sale for the Apple II, the first spreadsheet. Dan Bricklin conceived it watching a Harvard Business School professor erase and rewrite blackboard tables whenever one figure changed. On screen, an electronic grid recalculates every dependent cell when one entry changes, matching $20,000 financial modelling languages without learning any language. Businessmen who saw it bought $2,000 Apple IIs to run it, making it that machine’s killer app.

brac-oral-therapy-extension-1980.summary: From 1980 BRAC taught 12 million Bangladeshi mothers to mix a drink of water, salt and sugar; child deaths from diarrhoea fell. In February 1979, BRAC began a field trial in two villages of Sulla thana, and in 1980 scaled it up as its Oral Therapy Extension Programme. Its workers taught rural mothers in their own homes to mix oral rehydration solution from ingredients already in their kitchens and to use it when diarrhoea struck. Over ten years it reached 12 million households in 75,000 villages.

Fifteen years on, most mothers taught could still prepare safe solution, and rural households used it in over 80 percent of severe diarrhoea cases, a rate among the world’s highest.

chile-sx-ew-copper-1980.summary: Solvent extraction and electrowinning (SX-EW) leaches copper from crushed oxide ore with dilute sulphuric acid, concentrates it with organic extractants and plates it onto cathodes without smelting. Pioneered at Ranchers' Bluebird mine in Arizona in 1968, it moved to a far larger scale in Chile: Sociedad Minera Pudahuel's Lo Aguirre plant opened in 1980 with bacterial-assisted heap leaching, Codelco added SX-EW at Chuquicamata in 1987, and by the 1990s El Abra, Quebrada Blanca, Zaldívar and Radomiro Tomic ran some of the world's largest plants. By 2000 Chile produced about half of global SX-EW copper, around 1.4 million tonnes a year. Miners could treat dumps and oxide caps once left as waste, with lower capital cost and no sulphur dioxide emissions.
